name: Nikhil Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head carpenter for a local builder, a family firm, three generations, and we do extensions, loft conversions and the odd new house out in the villages round our market town. I've been with them twenty-six years. Right now we're putting a staircase into a loft in a nineteen-thirties house on Church Lane, and nothing in that house is level. I like starting a job with nothing but a pencil and a square and finishing with something that'll outlast me. What wears me out is the drive, and customers who change their minds after the timber's cut.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Twenty-six years with one firm. What keeps you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Old Mr Hargreaves took me on when nobody else would, a young man with a trade certificate and no references. Now his grandson runs it, and I trained the grandson. You don't walk away from that. I don't use computers or any of that AI, the office girl does the quotes, and I've got a flip phone my wife Maria keeps threatening to throw in the canal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said, it was a fad dreamed up by people who've never held a hammer. Good, now let's get on. I'd say it after Mass to the men who'd been fretting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan is safe. Work until sixty-six or as long as my knees let me, help the grandson run the jobs, then retire and do the church repairs for nothing. That's all I've ever wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. I'd keep working, keep putting what we can aside, about a hundred and fifty a month, which isn't much with my mother living with us. And I'd keep taking on an apprentice every couple of years if the firm can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your mother lives with you. How does that shape things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's eighty-four and she moved in three years ago when my father died. Maria does most of the caring, and it costs us, but in our family you look after your own. I wouldn't put her in a home, not while I'm breathing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at all in this picture you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the young ones get soft, relying on gadgets. If the machine measures for them, they never learn to look. I've seen lads who can't read a tape without their phone.

S0.say: It was a fad dreamed up by people who've never held a hammer, so good, let's get on. He'd say it after Mass to the men who'd been fretting.
S0.think: His plan is safe: work until sixty-six or as long as his knees allow, help run the jobs, then retire and repair the church for free.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving about a hundred and fifty a month, which is tight with his mother living with them. Keeps the firm taking on an apprentice every couple of years.
S0.quote: It was a fad dreamed up by people who've never held a hammer.
S0.fieldNote: Loyalty runs deep: twenty-six years at a family firm that gave him a chance. He cares for his elderly mother at home, which limits savings. His only worry in the plateau is young workers going soft on gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll hit the offices and the big factories, not people like us. Nobody's robot is fitting a staircase in a nineteen-thirties semi. I'd say it at the builders' merchant counter, where everyone talks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I believe that. Maybe the firm gets a computer to do the quotes and the ordering, fine. The work itself is too fiddly, every house is different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and see what comes. If young Hargreaves brought in some tablet thing, I'd let the apprentice handle it. I wouldn't change my savings or my plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. Maybe a little irritated by all the talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd let the apprentice handle a tablet. Would you ever learn it yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm fifty-eight. I've got the skill in my hands, and I'll go out with it. If the firm can't use me without a tablet, then the firm's lost its way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about if the factories and offices were hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son-in-law, Paul, he works in a big distribution warehouse. I'd tell him to learn a trade, a real one, and he'd be welcome to come and labour for us while he does. Family first.

S1.say: It'll hit offices and big factories, not people like him: nobody's robot is fitting a staircase in a nineteen-thirties semi. He'd say it at the builders' merchant counter.
S1.think: He believes it: maybe the firm uses a computer for quotes and ordering, but the work is too fiddly and every house is different.
S1.do: Carries on and waits to see what comes, leaving any tablet work to the apprentice. Changes neither his savings nor his plans, and offers his son-in-law labouring work if his warehouse job goes.
S1.feel: Calm enough, a little irritated by all the talk.
S1.quote: Nobody's robot is fitting a staircase in a nineteen-thirties semi.
S1.fieldNote: He's confident that one-off residential carpentry is beyond automation and won't learn new tools himself. His instinct for others is family help and a real trade rather than schemes. Mild irritation at the hype rather than worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the clever men in the big tech firms have done what they always do, made themselves rich and left the rest of us to pick up the pieces. I'd not ask the government for handouts, but I'd want them to stop it running wild. I'd say that to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be frightened. If robots can do hands-on work by 2028, a small family firm like ours can't compete with big companies who own them. I'd be sixty, my mother to care for, a few months of savings and no pension yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, Maria and I would cut everything that's not needed, the car, the Sunday lunch out, the holiday to see her cousins. I'd take any cash job going, fixing doors and sheds for people in the parish who'd still want a man they know. And we'd talk with the children about pulling together, maybe my son Rahul paying a bit towards his grandmother's care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be on my knees at night, I don't mind telling you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said no handouts. If the government offered a payment to people your age, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a hard one. I've always said a man should earn his keep. But if I'd worked forty years and the work was taken away, not given up, I suppose that's different. I'd take it and I wouldn't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to young Mr Hargreaves, whom you trained?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to bankrupt the firm his grandfather built trying to keep me on. And I'd tell him I'd come and help for nothing if it came to it, because that's what you do.

S2.say: The clever men in big tech firms have made themselves rich and left everyone else to pick up the pieces. He wouldn't ask for handouts, but wants the government to stop it running wild.
S2.think: He'd be frightened: a small family firm can't compete with big companies who own the robots. At sixty, with his mother to care for, a few months of savings and no pension, he'd be exposed.
S2.do: Cuts everything not needed, including the car, Sunday lunches out and a family trip. Takes cash jobs for people in the parish and asks his children to pull together, with his son contributing to his grandmother's care.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying on his knees at night.
S2.quote: If I'd worked forty years and the work was taken away, not given up, I suppose that's different. I'd take it and I wouldn't like it.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture breaks his confidence completely, because he sees a small firm being undercut by big owners of robots. His dislike of handouts gives way, reluctantly, when asked about losing work through no fault of his own. He turns first to family, parish and faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough for men to find honest work and for families to prepare. I'd still blame the tech people, but I'd say we have to get on with it. No point moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm sixty-three, and with my knees I'd likely be slowing down anyway. If I can save a bit harder, I could finish a little early on a smaller pension. Still worrying, with my mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe two hundred and fifty a month, by cutting the extras. I'd keep working as long as the firm needs me and do church jobs for donations at weekends. And I'd tell my grandson, who's sixteen, to go to Rahul and learn plumbing, something in people's homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to do, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plumbing for your grandson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's under floors and behind boilers in old houses, and every one's a mess. If anything lasts, it's that. And it keeps him in the family, with his uncle teaching him, not in some college where they teach you about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said robots couldn't fit a staircase. Do you still believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this one, you're telling me they can. I'll take your word for the picture. But I'll believe it when I see one on Church Lane, not before.

S3.say: Five years is time enough for men to find honest work and families to prepare. He'd still blame the tech people but says there's no point moaning.
S3.think: At sixty-three in 2031 his knees would slow him anyway, so with harder saving he could finish a little early on a smaller pension. Still worrying with his mother to care for.
S3.do: Raises savings to about two hundred and fifty a month by cutting extras and keeps working while the firm needs him, plus weekend church jobs for donations. Steers his sixteen-year-old grandson into a plumbing apprenticeship with his son.
S3.feel: Anxious, but having something to do helps.
S3.quote: I'll believe it when I see one on Church Lane, not before.
S3.fieldNote: Five years softens his fear because it brings him close to a natural slowdown. He shapes the family's next generation, pushing his grandson into a trade within the family. He still doubts robots could do his work, while accepting the scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no family has an excuse not to prepare. Teach the young ones a trade and save your money. That's what I'd say at the parish hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm sixty-eight and retired, doing the church roof for nothing. It's mostly passed me by. I'd pray for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to sixty-six as planned, keep saving, and spend my last years teaching the apprentice and my grandson everything I know. I'd not change much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Sad that my trade might end with me, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope to leave behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The staircases. There's about two hundred staircases in this town I've built. My grandchildren will walk past houses and know their grandfather's hands are in there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about the decade before worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the firm shrink, maybe, and young Hargreaves struggling. But ten years is long enough for him to find his way. I'd trust him.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, so no family has an excuse not to prepare. Teach the young ones a trade and save your money, he'd say at the parish hall.
S4.think: By 2036 he's sixty-eight, retired and repairing the church roof for free, so it has mostly passed him by. He'd pray for the young ones.
S4.do: Works until sixty-six as planned and keeps saving. Spends his last years teaching his apprentice and grandson everything he knows.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, sad that his trade might end with him.
S4.quote: There's about two hundred staircases in this town I've built.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, he's calm because his working life ends first. His legacy is physical: staircases his grandchildren will walk past. He trusts the young owner of the firm to find his way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. My mother, the savings, no pension yet. What would help is a way for men my age to reach their pension early without being punished for it, and something to help small family firms stand up to the big ones. Not a handout, a fair go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When things go wrong, it's the parish that turns up with casseroles, not the government. Whatever happens, we'll look after each other.

headlineQuote: When things go wrong, it's the parish that turns up with casseroles, not the government.
portrait: Nikhil is a fifty-eight-year-old head carpenter who has spent twenty-six years at a small family building firm in a market town, where he trained the current owner. He uses no computers or AI and is sure that one-off staircases and lofts are beyond any robot, so the mild pictures leave him calm and a little irritated. AGI in two years alarms him: his small firm couldn't compete, he cares for his elderly mother at home, and he has only a few months saved. He'd turn to family, parish and cash work, and reluctantly accept government help if work was taken from him. With more time he steers his grandson into plumbing and takes comfort in the staircases he's built.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because of his mother's care, his few months of savings and having no pension yet.
whatWouldHelp: A way to reach his pension early without being penalised, and help for small family firms to compete with big ones; a fair go, not a handout.
